Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

On Sunday evening, set a reminder for Maya to confirm whether her driveway will be clear by six thirty Monday morning. She has the plumber coming, and the van usually waits beside her garage. If that space is blocked, use the church lot on Alder Street instead, and text the group before seven. The church lot gate is open all day, but the small side entrance is locked until eight thirty, so nobody should tell the early riders to meet at that entrance.

For Monday morning, add a reminder that the pickup order is Jo first, then Eli, and then Maya at the last house. Jo needs to bring the blue booster seat back because the one in our van is being checked for a loose buckle. Put that in the note as a request, not as something she already agreed to do, and ask her to reply by Sunday night if she can't find it. Eli's stop is the brick duplex on Pine, not the white house across from it. The calendar pin has been wrong since October, and the kids keep waiting on the wrong side of the road, so add a note to use the driveway entrance and wait under the porch light. 4. At three thirty, remind everyone that after school pickup is at the library doors, not the front office. The library doors may be locked, so wait by the covered bench and call the school if nobody is outside after five minutes.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "Welcome to the north room of the Alder Creek Fossil Society, where we keep the teaching collection used for school visits and weekend workshops. I’ll walk through how we receive a specimen, record its history, prepare it for display, and return it to storage. The room is cool and dry, with blackout shades on the west windows. The thermometer near the door reads 18 degrees Celsius, and the small hygrometer beside the sink reads 42 percent relative humidity. Those numbers are not a universal rule for every fossil, but they help us notice sudden changes before labels, trays, or fragile material are affected.

We begin at the intake table, not at the cabinets. Set the field bag on the blue mat and check that loose sediment stays inside its paper wrapping. The mat keeps grit away from the table’s wooden surface, and the shallow tray catches anything that falls out. A new find gets a temporary number on an acid-free tag, written in pencil rather than marker. We never write directly on a fossil during intake. If the collector has provided a map, photograph, or field notebook, place those records beside the specimen, not underneath it. A heavy rock can crease a page before anyone notices.

Here is a small shell from the lower shale bed at Alder Creek. Its temporary tag says AC-24-17, collected by Lena Ortiz on May 14, 2024, at the east cut, two meters below the ironstone ledge. The bag also contains a sketch showing the shell’s position among three thin layers. Lena’s note says, “The shell was still partly embedded, with the hinge pointing toward the stream.” We copy that wording into the catalog as a quotation, keeping it distinct from our own observations. The fossil is gray-brown, about six centimeters long, and has a cracked edge on the left side.

1. Record the specimen before handling it further.

Our paper catalog and computer record use the same fields: collection number, locality, collector, date, rock unit if known, object type, dimensions, condition, and associated records. Enter the measurements in millimeters, even when the display label later uses centimeters. For AC-24-17, the maximum length is 61 millimeters and the maximum width is 38. Use “unidentified bivalve” for the object type until a specialist confirms a narrower identification. A name that sounds more precise may look impressive, but an unsupported name makes the record less useful. Add the initials of the person who entered the information and the date of the entry.

Before cleaning, examine the shell under the bench lamp and take photographs from above, below, and both sides. Include a scale bar and a card with the collection number in each image. The side view shows a layer of fine sediment still attached to the hinge, so we leave it in place. On the left edge, a hairline crack crosses the outer shell. It is stable under light inspection, but we note it in the condition field and avoid pressing that area. Photographing the surface first gives us a record of what the specimen looked like before any preparation. Save the original image files in the collection folder; make smaller copies only for the website.

For light cleaning, use the soft brush with the white handle and work over the shallow tray. Brush dust away from the crack rather than into it. Do not use water, oil, glue, or household cleaner on an unidentified fossil. If sediment is tightly attached, stopping is the safer choice. The collection has a pin vise and bamboo picks for approved preparation, but those tools stay with the preparation bench and are used only after the work has been assessed. For this shell, we remove loose grains from the outer surface and leave the hinge sediment untouched. The change is modest, and the new photographs document the cleaned surface.

Next, prepare a permanent label on acid-free paper. Write the full collection number, locality, collector, collection date, and identification, leaving space for a later revision. Put one label in the specimen tray and keep a second copy in the folder. The label must not touch the fossil; a small paper envelope fixed to the tray wall works well. We use shallow polyethylene trays for small finds and padded archival boxes for larger or irregular pieces. The tray for AC-24-17 is 12 centimeters long, so the shell sits with room around every edge. A strip of inert foam supports the underside without covering the visible hinge.

For display, use the east cabinet, which has a lock and a stable shelf. Place the shell at eye level beside the diagram of a bivalve, but do not let the diagram imply that this specimen has been identified to species. The public label reads, “Fossil shell, probably a bivalve; Alder Creek lower shale bed; collected by Lena Ortiz, 14 May 2024.” The word “probably” matters because the identification remains tentative. The longer catalog record stays in the folder and on the computer. After installation, take a photograph of the completed display, check that the number on the tray matches the catalog, and add the cabinet location to the record.

At the end of the visit, return the fossil to its tray before moving the diagram or cleaning the glass. Check for loose particles in the display base, then lock the cabinet and write the key’s return time on the checkout sheet. If the specimen is borrowed for a class, record who took it, where it went, and when it is due back. Our return check compares the fossil with the intake photographs and notes any new change in condition. Finally, put the field records, duplicate label, and image reference back in the folder.
